title: Progressive Waves
short_intro: A progressive wave is a disturbance that travels continuously through a medium, transferring energy and momentum from one point to another without permanent displacement of the medium particles. It is characterized by a continuous phase change along the direction of propagation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of wavelength, frequency, wave velocity, phase relation, displacement equation of a harmonic progressive wave, and relation between particle velocity and wave velocity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential wave equation, energy density, intensity of progressive waves, acoustic impedance, spherical and cylindrical wave forms, and phase velocity versus group velocity.

prerequisites: Elastic properties of media (Young's modulus, bulk modulus)

concept_notes.heading: Characteristics of Progressive Waves
bullets: All particles of the medium execute simple harmonic motion of the same amplitude and frequency about their mean positions.
Phase of vibration changes continuously from one particle to the next along the direction of wave travel.
Energy is transmitted across the medium at a constant rate known as wave velocity.
Particles possess maximum velocity at their respective mean positions and zero velocity at extreme positions.

concept_notes.heading: Mathematical Representation
bullets: A plane progressive wave travelling along the positive x-axis is represented as y(x,t) = A sin(ωt - kx + φ).
The angular frequency is given by ω = 2πf and the propagation constant (wave number) is k = 2π / λ.
The argument (ωt - kx + φ) represents the phase of the wave at position x and time t.

concept_notes.heading: Particle Velocity versus Wave Velocity
bullets: Wave velocity (v) is the speed at which the phase or disturbance travels through the medium, depending on elastic and inertial properties.
Particle velocity (v_p) is the instantaneous velocity of a medium particle executing SHM, obtained by differentiating displacement with respect to time.
The relation between particle velocity and wave velocity is given by v_p = - (slope of displacement curve) × (wave velocity).

concept_notes.heading: Energy and Intensity in Progressive Waves
bullets: A progressive wave carries kinetic and potential energy per unit volume through the medium.
Energy density E is proportional to the square of the amplitude (A) and square of the frequency (f).
Intensity (I) is defined as the average energy transmitted per unit time per unit area normal to the direction of wave propagation.

derivations.title: Differential Equation of a Progressive Wave
derivations.conditions: Homogeneous, isotropic, perfectly elastic medium obeying Hooke's law
steps: Start with the harmonic progressive wave equation y = A sin(ωt - kx).
Differentiate displacement y partially twice with respect to time t to get ∂²y / ∂t² = -ω²y.
Differentiate displacement y partially twice with respect to position x to get ∂²y / ∂x² = -k²y.
Combine the two derivatives using the relation v = ω / k to eliminate frequency and wave number.

derivations.title: Relation between Phase Difference and Path Difference
derivations.conditions: Harmonic progressive wave travelling in a uniform medium
steps: Consider two points separated by a path difference Δx.
A complete wavelength (λ) corresponds to a phase change of 2π radians.
Set up the direct proportionality between phase difference (Δφ) and path difference (Δx): Δφ / 2π = Δx / λ.
Solve for Δφ to obtain the final standard formula.

formula_sheet.name: Progressive Wave Displacement
formula_sheet.variables: y = displacement, A = amplitude, ω = angular frequency, k = wave number

formula_sheet.name: Wave Velocity / Phase Velocity
formula_sheet.variables: f = frequency, λ = wavelength, ω = angular frequency, k = wave number

formula_sheet.name: Particle Velocity
formula_sheet.equation_html: v_p = \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} = A \omega \cos(\omega t - kx)
formula_sheet.variables: v_p = particle velocity, Aω = maximum particle velocity
formula_sheet.conditions: Any point on the progressive wave

formula_sheet.name: Maximum Particle Velocity
formula_sheet.variables: A = amplitude, ω = angular frequency, f = frequency

formula_sheet.name: Energy Density of a Wave
formula_sheet.equation_html: E = 2 \pi^2 m \nu^2 A^2 \text{ or } E = \rho A^2 \omega^2
formula_sheet.variables: E = total energy per unit volume, ρ = density of medium, A = amplitude, ω = angular frequency
formula_sheet.conditions: Plane progressive wave in elastic medium

formula_sheet.name: Intensity of Wave
formula_sheet.variables: I = intensity, ρ = density, v = wave speed, ω = angular frequency, A = amplitude

formula_sheet.name: Differential Wave Equation
formula_sheet.variables: y = displacement, v = wave velocity, t = time, x = position

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Distance (y-x) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal wave profile showing displacement y on the vertical axis and position x on the horizontal axis at a fixed instant t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Gives a snapshot of the wave. The horizontal distance between two consecutive crests or troughs represents the wavelength (λ).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested for identifying wavelength, amplitude, and instantaneous spatial variation of phase.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time (y-t) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal curve plotting displacement y against time t for a fixed particle position x.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the simple harmonic motion of a single particle in the medium. The time period (T) is read directly along the time axis.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate particle frequency, time period, and maximum particle velocity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kundt's Tube Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal glass tube containing lycopodium powder with a vibrating rod at one end and a movable piston at the other.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The powder collects in heaps at the nodes due to acoustic radiation pressure in standing waves formed by superposition, allowing measurement of wavelength.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptually linked to progressive wave reflection and sound velocity determination in gases.

solved_numericals.question: A progressive wave is represented by the equation y = 0.05 sin(200πt - 4πx), where x and y are in meters and t is in seconds. Calculate the frequency and wave velocity.
solution_steps: Compare the given equation y = 0.05 sin(200πt - 4πx) with the standard wave equation y = A sin(ωt - kx).
Identify angular frequency ω = 200π rad/s and wave number k = 4π rad/m.
Calculate wave velocity v = ω / k = 200π / (4π) = 50 m/s.
solved_numericals.answer: Frequency = 100 Hz, Wave velocity = 50 m s^{-1}

solved_numericals.question: The displacement of a particle in a progressive wave is given by y = 0.02 sin(50t - x), with units in SI. Find the maximum particle velocity and the ratio of maximum particle velocity to wave velocity.
solution_steps: Identify A = 0.02 m, ω = 50 rad/s, and k = 1 rad/m from y = 0.02 sin(50t - x).
Calculate maximum particle velocity v_{max} = Aω = 0.02 × 50 = 1.0 m/s.
Calculate wave velocity v = ω / k = 50 / 1 = 50 m/s.
solved_numericals.answer: Maximum particle velocity = 1.0 m s^{-1}, Ratio = 0.02

solved_numericals.question: Two points on a progressive wave have a path difference of 0.5 m. If the frequency of the wave is 150 Hz and the wave velocity is 300 m/s, find the phase difference between these two points.
solution_steps: Substitute λ = 2 m and path difference Δx = 0.5 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the medium is homogeneous, isotropic, and perfectly elastic, which is an idealization not fully realized in real fluids or solids.
Applies linear wave theory (small amplitude approximation), valid only when particle velocities are much smaller than the wave propagation velocity so that Hooke's law holds strictly.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Medium particles travel forward along with the progressive wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: Particles only oscillate back and forth about their fixed mean positions while energy is transferred.
common_misconceptions.why: Wave motion is a propagation of state and energy, not bulk transport of matter.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All particles in a progressive wave have the same velocity at any given instant.
common_misconceptions.correct: Particles have different velocities depending on their instantaneous phase in SHM.
common_misconceptions.why: Phase varies continuously with position x along the wave path.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particle velocity and wave velocity are physically the same quantity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Particle velocity depends on the time derivative of particle displacement, whereas wave velocity depends on elastic and inertial properties of the medium.
common_misconceptions.why: They represent completely different kinematic and dynamic phenomena.

quick_revision: Plane progressive wave equation: y = A sin(ωt - kx)
Intensity is directly proportional to the square of amplitude and square of frequency.
